claim: Object concepts are represented in a feature-based manner, incorporating observable perceptual properties and abstract conceptual features.
source: Many neurocognitive models of semantic memory incorporate the notion that object concepts are represented in a feature-based manner (Rosch and Mervis, 1975; Tyler and Moss, 2001; Rogers and McClelland, 2004). On this view, our understanding of the concept 'hairdryer' is thought to reflect knowledge of observable perceptual properties (e.g. visual form) and abstract conceptual features (e.g. 'used to style hair').
evidence: Supported by citations to established theoretical frameworks (Rosch and Mervis, 1975; Tyler and Moss, 2001; Rogers and McClelland, 2004)

claim: There is not always a one-to-one correspondence between how something looks and what it is.
source: Importantly, there is not always a one-to-one correspondence between how something looks and what it is; a hairdryer and a comb are conceptually similar despite being visually distinct, whereas a hairdryer and a gun are conceptually distinct despite being visually similar.
evidence: Supported by examples illustrating dissociation between visual and conceptual similarity

claim: A fully-specified representation of an object concept requires integration of its perceptual and conceptual features.
source: Thus, a fully-specified representation of an object concept (i.e. one that can be distinguished from any and all other concepts), requires integration of its perceptual and conceptual features.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that visual and conceptual features can vary independently

claim: Object features are coded in the modality-specific cortical regions that supported their processing at the time of acquisition.
source: Neuroimaging research suggests that object features are coded in the modality-specific cortical regions that supported their processing at the time of acquisition (Thompson-Schill, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to neuroimaging research

claim: Knowledge about the visual form of an object concept is coded in occipito-temporal visual processing regions.
source: For example, knowledge about the visual form of an object concept is thought to be coded in occipito-temporal visual processing regions (Martin and Chao, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Some theories propose that distributed feature representations emerge through interactions among modality-specific cortical areas.
source: On one view, these representations are thought to emerge through interactions among modality-specific cortical areas (Kiefer and Pulvermüller, 2012; Martin, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical frameworks

claim: Competing theories propose that distributed feature representations reflect integration of modality-specific features in trans-modal convergence zones.
source: Within a competing class of theories, they are thought to reflect the integration of modality-specific features in trans-modal convergence zones (Damasio, 1989; Rogers et al., 2004; Binder and Desai, 2011), such as the anterior temporal lobes (ATL) (Patterson et al., 2007; Tranel, 2009; Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical frameworks

claim: Semantic dementia is characterized by progressive loss of conceptual knowledge across all receptive and expressive modalities.
source: Behaviorally, SD is characterized by the progressive loss of conceptual knowledge across all receptive and expressive modalities (Warrington, 1975; Hodges et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuropsychological research

claim: Semantic dementia is associated with extensive atrophy of the anterior temporal lobe, with earliest and most pronounced volume loss in the left temporal pole.
source: At the level of neuropathology, SD is associated with extensive atrophy of the ATL, with the earliest and most pronounced volume loss in the left temporal pole (Mummery et al., 2000; Galton et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuropathological studies

claim: Patients with semantic dementia tend to confuse conceptually similar objects that are visually distinct, but not visually similar objects that are conceptually distinct.
source: Most important from a theoretical perspective, patients with SD tend to confuse conceptually similar objects that are visually distinct (e.g. hairdryer – comb), but not visually similar objects that are conceptually distinct (e.g., hairdryer – gun), indicating that the temporal pole expresses conceptual similarity structure (Graham et al., 1994; see Peelen and Caramazza, 2012; Chadwick et al., 2016, for related neuroimaging evidence).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies

claim: The temporal pole supports multi-modal integration of abstract conceptual, but not perceptual, features.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the temporal pole supports multi-modal integration of abstract conceptual, but not perceptual, features.
evidence: Inference drawn from cited neuropsychological and neuroimaging evidence

claim: The representational-hierarchical model proposes that perirhinal cortex supports integration of conceptual and perceptual features.
source: The representational-hierarchical model of object coding emphasizes a role for perirhinal cortex (PRC), located in the medial ATL, in feature integration that is distinct from that of the temporal pole (Murray and Bussey, 1999). Namely, within this framework PRC is thought to support the integration of conceptual and perceptual features.
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical framework

claim: Object representations in perirhinal cortex have been described in terms of conceptual feature conjunctions in studies of semantic memory.
source: In line with this view, object representations in PRC have been described in terms of conceptual feature conjunctions in studies of semantic memory (Moss et al., 2005; Bruffaerts et al., 2013; Clarke and Tyler, 2014; 2015; Wright et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Object representations in perirhinal cortex have been described in terms of visual feature conjunctions in studies of visual processing.
source: and visual feature conjunctions in studies of visual processing (Barense et al., 2005; 2007; 2012; Lee et al., 2005; Devlin and Price, 2007; Murray et al., 2007; O'Neil et al., 2009; Graham et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: It is difficult to synthesize results from parallel lines of research on perirhinal cortex because conceptual and perceptual features tend to vary concomitantly across stimuli.
source: However, it is difficult to synthesize results from these parallel lines of research, in part, because conceptual and perceptual features tend to vary concomitantly across stimuli (Mur, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation and logical reasoning

claim: Direct evidence of integration across conceptual and perceptual features in perirhinal cortex remains elusive.
source: Thus, although the representational-hierarchical account was initially formalized nearly two decades ago (Murray and Bussey, 1999), direct evidence of integration across conceptual and perceptual features remains elusive.
evidence: Assessment of the state of the literature

claim: The behavior-based visual RDM and behavior-based conceptual RDM were not significantly correlated with one another.
source: Critically, this analysis revealed that the model RDMs were not significantly correlated with one another (Kendall's tau-a = 0.01, p=0.10), indicating that differences in visual and conceptual features were not confounded across object concepts.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data

claim: The word2vec RDM was significantly correlated with the behavior-based conceptual RDM.
source: Importantly, the word2vec RDM was significantly correlated with our behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.11, SE = 0.0141, p<0.00001), suggesting that both models captured the conceptual similarity structure among the object concepts.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: The word2vec RDM was significantly correlated with the behavior-based visual RDM.
source: However, the word2vec RDM was also significantly correlated with our behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.04, SE = 0.0130, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: The behavior-based conceptual RDM captured semantic similarity selectively defined as conceptual object features, whereas the word2vec RDM captured a broader definition of semantic similarity including both visual semantics and abstract conceptual features.
source: This result suggests that, in line with our objectives, the behavior-based conceptual RDM captured semantic similarity selectively defined as conceptual object features, whereas the word2vec RDM may have captured a broader definition of semantic similarity, that is, one that includes both visual semantics and abstract conceptual features.
evidence: Inference drawn from statistical comparisons

claim: All participants provided the same yes/no response to the property verification task on 88.4% of all trials.
source: Behavioral performance on the scanned property verification task indicated that participants interpreted the object concepts and property verification probes with a high degree of consistency (Figure 3). Specifically, all participants (i.e. 16/16) provided the same yes/no response to the property verification task on 88.4% of all trials.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from fMRI task

claim: Agreement was highest for the 'living' verification probe (96.8%) and lowest for the 'non-tool' verification probe (73.2%).
source: Agreement was highest for the 'living' verification probe (96.8%) and lowest for the 'non-tool' verification probe (73.2%).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from fMRI task

claim: The proportion of trials on which all participants provided the same response did not differ between the visual feature verification task context and the conceptual feature verification task context.
source: Moreover, the proportion of trials on which all participants provided the same response did not differ between the visual feature verification task context (mean = 87.3% collapsed across all eight visual probes) and the conceptual feature verification task context (mean = 89.5% collapsed across all eight conceptual probes) (z = 0.19, p=0.85).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data

claim: Response latencies were comparable across the visual feature verification task context and the conceptual feature verification task context.
source: Response latencies were also comparable across the visual feature verification task context (mean = 1361 ms, SD = 303) and the conceptual feature verification task context (mean = 1376 ms, SD = 315) (t (15)=1.00, p=0.33, 95% CI [−49.09, 17.71).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data

claim: Lateral occipital cortex represents object concepts in a task-dependent visual similarity code.
source: Consistent with its well-established role in the processing of visual form, patterns of activity within LOC reflected the visual similarity of the object concepts (Figure 6A). Specifically, the brain-based visual task RDMs obtained across participants in LOC were significantly correlated with the behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.045, p<0.002), but not the behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = −0.006, p=0.72).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Activity patterns in lateral occipital cortex expressed neither visual nor conceptual similarity structure when participants made judgments that pertained to conceptual object features.
source: By contrast, the brain-based conceptual task RDMs obtained across participants in LOC were not significantly correlated with either the behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.006, p=0.13) or the behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.003, p=0.65).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Parahippocampal cortex represents object concepts in a task-dependent conceptual similarity code.
source: Patterns of activity obtained in parahippocampal cortex, which has previously been associated with the processing of semantically-based contextual associations (Bar and Aminoff, 2003; Aminoff et al., 2013), reflected the conceptual similarity of the object concepts (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data and citations

claim: Activity patterns in parahippocampal cortex expressed neither visual nor conceptual similarity structure when participants made judgments that pertained to visual object features.
source: First, the brain-based visual task RDMs obtained across participants in parahippocampal cortex were not significantly correlated with either the behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.005, p=0.26) or the behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.009, p=0.26).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Activity patterns in parahippocampal cortex expressed conceptual similarity structure when participants made judgments about conceptual features.
source: Second, the brain-based conceptual task RDMs obtained across participants in parahippocampal cortex were not significantly related to the behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = −0.008, p=0.55), but they were correlated with the behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.046, p<0.002).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: The temporal pole represents object concepts in a task-invariant conceptual similarity code.
source: In line with theoretical frameworks that have characterized the temporal pole as a semantic hub (Patterson et al., 2007; Tranel, 2009), patterns of activity within this specific ATL structure reflected the conceptual similarity of the object concepts (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data and citations to theoretical frameworks

claim: Brain-based visual task RDMs in the temporal pole were correlated with the behavior-based conceptual RDM but not the behavior-based visual RDM.
source: Specifically, whereas the brain-based visual task RDMs obtained across participants in the temporal pole were not significantly correlated with the behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.006, p=0.25), they were correlated with the behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.035, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Brain-based conceptual task RDMs in the temporal pole were correlated with the behavior-based conceptual RDM but not the behavior-based visual RDM.
source: Similarly, whereas the brain-based conceptual task RDMs obtained across participants in the temporal pole were not significantly correlated with the behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.0005, p=0.47), they were correlated with the behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.05, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Perirhinal cortex represents object concepts in a task-invariant similarity code that reflects integration of visual and conceptual features.
source: Results obtained in PRC support the notion that this structure integrates visual and conceptual object features (6C), as first theorized in the representational-hierarchical model of object representation (Murray and Bussey, 1999). Namely, we revealed that the brain-based visual task RDMs obtained across participants in PRC were significantly correlated with both the behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.052, p<0.0001), and the behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.036, p<0.0003). Similarly, the brain-based conceptual task RDMs obtained across participants were also correlated with both the behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.035, p<0.002), and the behavior-based conceptual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.057, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data and citation to theoretical framework

claim: The word2vec RDM was significantly correlated with brain-based conceptual task RDMs in parahippocampal cortex, perirhinal cortex, and the temporal pole.
source: These analyses revealed significant positive correlations between the word2vec RDM and the brain-based conceptual task RDMs in parahippocampal cortex (Kendall's tau-a = 0.05, p<0.01), PRC (Kendall's tau-a = 0.035, p<0.01), and the temporal pole (Kendall's tau-a = 0.029, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: The word2vec RDM was significantly correlated with brain-based visual task RDMs in perirhinal cortex and the temporal pole.
source: The word2vec RDM was also significantly correlated with the brain-based visual task RDMs in PRC (Kendall's tau-a = 0.025, p<0.05) and the temporal pole (Kendall's tau-a = 0.027, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: The word2vec RDM was significantly correlated with brain-based visual task RDMs in lateral occipital cortex.
source: Interestingly, however, the word2vec RDM was also significantly correlated with the brain-based visual task RDMs in LOC (Kendall's tau-a = 0.028, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Brain-based visual task RDMs and brain-based conceptual task RDMs were significantly correlated in perirhinal cortex.
source: Importantly, we found a significant positive correlation in PRC (Kendall's tau-a = 0.063, p<0.0001), and a trend toward a significant correlation in the temporal pole (Kendall's tau-a = 0.032, p=0.012).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Brain-based visual and conceptual task RDMs were not significantly correlated in parahippocampal cortex or lateral occipital cortex.
source: Conversely, brain-based visual and conceptual task RDMs were not significantly correlated in either parahippocampal cortex (Kendall's tau-a = 0.008, p=0.12), or LOC (Kendall's tau-a = −0.008, p=0.92).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Brain-based visual task RDMs obtained across different ROIs were not significantly correlated with each other.
source: Interestingly, these analyses did not reveal any significant results between any of our ROIs (all Kendall's tau-a <0.01, all p>0.07).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Brain-based conceptual task RDMs obtained across different ROIs were not significantly correlated with each other.
source: This set of analyses did not reveal any significant results between any of our ROIs (all Kendall's tau-a <0.016, all p>0.012).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Within-object similarity did not differ from zero in lateral occipital cortex.
source: Within-object similarity did not differ from zero in either LOC (Pearson's r = 0.007, p=0.20) or parahippocampal cortex (Pearson's r = −0.008, p=0.87), suggesting that a given object concept was represented differently across the visual and conceptual task contexts in these ROIs.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: Within-object similarity did not differ from zero in parahippocampal cortex.
source: Within-object similarity did not differ from zero in either LOC (Pearson's r = 0.007, p=0.20) or parahippocampal cortex (Pearson's r = −0.008, p=0.87), suggesting that a given object concept was represented differently across the visual and conceptual task contexts in these ROIs.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: Within-object similarity was significantly greater than zero in the temporal pole.
source: Conversely, within-object similarity was significantly greater than zero in the temporal pole (Pearson's r = 0.34, p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected for four comparisons), indicating that this structure represents a given object concept similarly across different task contexts.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: Within-object similarity was significantly greater than zero in perirhinal cortex.
source: Within-object similarity was also significantly greater than zero in PRC (Pearson's r = 0.41, p<0.01, Bonferroni corrected for four comparisons), again indicating that a given object concept was represented similarly across different task contexts.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: Searchlight analysis revealed evidence for visual similarity coding in the visual task context in aspects of right lateral occipital cortex, early visual cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and areas of medial and lateral ventral temporal cortex.
source: First, we found evidence for visual similarity coding in the visual task context in aspects of right LOC (Figure 9A), as well as aspects of early visual cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and areas of medial and lateral ventral temporal cortex (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by searchlight RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Searchlight analysis revealed conceptual similarity coding in the conceptual task context within a cluster of voxels that straddled the border between right parahippocampal cortex and perirhinal cortex.
source: Next, we revealed conceptual similarity coding in the conceptual task context within a cluster of voxels that straddled the border between right parahippocampal cortex and PRC (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by searchlight RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: Searchlight analysis revealed evidence of conceptual similarity coding in bilateral aspects of the temporal pole in both task contexts.
source: Moreover, we found evidence of conceptual similarity coding in bilateral aspects of the temporal pole in both task contexts (Figures 9B and 10B), an observation that is consistent with results from multiple prior studies that have demonstrated conceptual similarity structure this aspect of the ATL (Peelen and Caramazza, 2012; Chadwick et al., 2016; cf Fairhall and Caramazza, 2013).
evidence: Supported by searchlight RSA analysis of fMRI data and citations to prior research

claim: Searchlight analysis revealed evidence for visual similarity coding and conceptual similarity coding in perirhinal cortex in both task contexts.
source: Finally, and most importantly, results from the whole-brain searchlight revealed evidence for visual similarity coding and conceptual similarity coding in PRC in both task contexts (Figures 9 and 10).
evidence: Supported by searchlight RSA analysis of fMRI data

claim: A contiguous cluster of voxels unique to left perirhinal cortex showed both visual and conceptual similarity coding in the visual task context.
source: Importantly, we revealed a contiguous cluster of voxels that was unique to left PRC in which both behavior-based RDMs predicted the similarity structure in the brain-based visual task RDMs.
evidence: Supported by voxel overlap analysis of searchlight RSA results

claim: A contiguous cluster of voxels unique to left perirhinal cortex showed both visual and conceptual similarity coding in the conceptual task context.
source: This analysis also revealed a contiguous cluster of voxels that was unique to left PRC in which both behavior-based RDMs predicted the similarity structure in the brain-based conceptual task RDMs.
evidence: Supported by voxel overlap analysis of searchlight RSA results

claim: A contiguous cluster of voxels in left perirhinal cortex showed both visual and conceptual similarity coding in both the visual and conceptual task contexts.
source: This analysis revealed a contiguous cluster of voxels in left PRC in which both behavior-based RDMs predicted the similarity structure captured by both brain-based RDMs.
evidence: Supported by voxel overlap analysis of searchlight RSA results

claim: A subset of voxels unique to perirhinal cortex carried information about visual and conceptual object information regardless of whether task demands biased attention toward visual or conceptual object features.
source: This result indicated that a subset of voxels that were unique to PRC carried information about visual and conceptual object information regardless of whether task demands biased attention toward visual or conceptual object features.
evidence: Inference drawn from voxel overlap analysis results

claim: Perirhinal cortex carries both visual and conceptual object information in the same subset of voxels.
source: Ultimately, this pattern of results suggests that not only does PRC carry both visual and conceptual object information, but it does so in the same subset of voxels.
evidence: Inference drawn from voxel overlap analysis results

claim: Perirhinal cortex uniquely represents the visual and conceptual features that define fully specified object concepts in an integrated similarity code.
source: Several aspects of our data provide novel support for the notion that PRC uniquely represents the visual and conceptual features that define fully specified object concepts in an integrated similarity code.
evidence: Summary inference drawn from multiple analyses

claim: Perirhinal cortex was the only region of the brain in which both visual and conceptual object coding was revealed.
source: First, this was the only region of the brain in which both visual and conceptual object coding was revealed.
evidence: Summary of searchlight and ROI-based RSA results

claim: Visual and conceptual coding effects in perirhinal cortex were observed regardless of whether fMRI task demands biased attention toward visual or conceptual object features.
source: Moreover, these effects were observed regardless of whether fMRI task demands biased attention toward visual or conceptual object features.
evidence: Summary of RSA results across task contexts

claim: At the level of perirhinal cortex, it may not be possible to fully disentangle conceptual and perceptual information.
source: When considered together, these results suggest that, at the level of PRC, it may not be possible to fully disentangle conceptual and perceptual information.
evidence: Inference drawn from pattern of results showing integrative coding

claim: Fully specified object representations allow for discrimination among stimuli with extensive feature overlap, such as exemplars from the same category.
source: What is the behavioral relevance of fully specified object representations in which visual and conceptual features are integrated? It has previously been suggested that such representations allow for discrimination among stimuli with extensive feature overlap, such as exemplars from the same category (Murray and Bussey, 1999; Noppeney et al., 2007; Graham et al., 2010; Clarke and Tyler, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work

claim: Individuals with medial anterior temporal lobe lesions that include perirhinal cortex typically have more pronounced conceptual impairments related to living than non-living things.
source: In line with this view, individuals with medial ATL lesions that include PRC typically have more pronounced conceptual impairments related to living than non-living things (Warrington and Shallice, 1984; Moss et al., 1997; Bozeat et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to neuropsychological research

claim: Individuals with medial anterior temporal lobe lesions that include perirhinal cortex have more striking perceptual impairments for objects that are visually similar as compared to visually distinct.
source: and more striking perceptual impairments for objects that are visually similar as compared to visually distinct (Barense et al., 2007, Barense et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuropsychological research

claim: Functional MRI studies have demonstrated increased perirhinal cortex engagement for living as compared to non-living objects.
source: Functional MRI studies in neurologically healthy individuals have also demonstrated increased PRC engagement for living as compared to non-living objects (Moss et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to fMRI research

claim: Functional MRI studies have demonstrated increased perirhinal cortex engagement for known as compared to novel faces.
source: for known as compared to novel faces (Barense et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to fMRI research

claim: Functional MRI studies have demonstrated increased perirhinal cortex engagement for faces or conceptually meaningless stimuli with high feature overlap as compared to low feature overlap.
source: and for faces or conceptually meaningless stimuli with high feature overlap as compared to low feature overlap (O'Neil et al., 2009; Barense et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to fMRI research

claim: Perirhinal cortex has been linked to explicit recognition memory judgments when previously studied and novel items are from the same stimulus category.
source: For example, PRC has been linked to explicit recognition memory judgments when previously studied and novel items are from the same stimulus category (Martin et al., 2013; 2016; 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to memory research

claim: Perirhinal cortex has been linked to judgments about lifetime experience with a given object concept.
source: and when subjects make judgments about their lifetime of experience with a given object concept (Duke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to memory research

claim: A behavior-based conceptual similarity model predicted the similarity structure of neural activity patterns in the temporal pole, irrespective of task context.
source: Consistent with this idea, we have shown that a behavior-based conceptual similarity model predicted the similarity structure of neural activity patterns in the temporal pole, irrespective of task context.
evidence: Summary of RSA results in temporal pole

claim: Neural activity patterns associated with conceptually similar object concepts that are visually distinct were more comparable than were conceptually dissimilar concepts that are visually similar in the temporal pole, even when task demands required assessment of visual features.
source: Specifically, neural activity patterns associated with conceptually similar object concepts that are visually distinct (e.g. hairdryer – comb) were more comparable than were conceptually dissimilar concepts that are visually similar (e.g. hairdryer – gun), even when task demands required a critical assessment of visual features.
evidence: Summary of RSA results in temporal pole

claim: Results demonstrate a representational distinction between the temporal pole and perirhinal cortex.
source: This observation, together with results obtained in PRC, demonstrates a representational distinction between these ATL structures, a conclusion that dovetails with recent evidence indicating that this region is not functionally homogeneous (Binney et al., 2010; Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison of results across ROIs, supported by citations

claim: Some anterior temporal lobe sub-regions play a prominent role in task-invariant extraction of conceptual object properties (e.g., temporal pole), whereas others make differential contributions to task-invariant integration of perceptual and conceptual features (e.g., perirhinal cortex).
source: Ultimately, this outcome suggests that some ATL sub-regions play a prominent role in task-invariant extraction of conceptual object properties (e.g. temporal pole), whereas others appear to make differential contributions to the task-invariant integration of perceptual and conceptual features (e.g. PRC) (Ralph et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference drawn from pattern of results, supported by citations

claim: Perirhinal cortex is connected to the temporal pole, parahippocampal cortex, lateral occipital cortex, and nearly all other unimodal and polymodal sensory regions in neocortex.
source: Convergent evidence from studies of functional and structural connectivity in humans, non-human primates, and rodents have revealed that PRC is connected to the temporal pole, parahippocampal cortex, LOC, and nearly all other unimodal and polymodal sensory regions in neocortex (Suzuki and Amaral, 1994; Burwell and Amaral, 1998; Kahn et al., 2008; McLelland et al., 2014; Suzuki and Naya, 2014; Wang et al., 2016; Zhuo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to connectivity studies

claim: Perirhinal cortex has the connectivity properties that make it well suited to be a trans-modal convergence zone capable of integrating object features that are both visual and conceptual in nature.
source: Thus, PRC has the connectivity properties that make it well suited to be a trans-modal convergence zone capable of integrating object features that are both visual and conceptual in nature.
evidence: Inference drawn from connectivity evidence and current results

claim: Attention may modulate information both within and between the regions of interest examined.
source: Although speculative, results from the current study suggest that attention may modulate information both within and between the ROIs examined.
evidence: Speculative inference from pattern of results

claim: Visual similarity coding was observed in lateral occipital cortex only when task demands biased attention to visual object features.
source: First, we see visual similarity coding in LOC only when task demands biased attention to visual object features, and conceptual similarity coding in parahippocampal cortex only when task demands biased attention to conceptual object features.
evidence: Summary of task-dependent effects in LOC

claim: Conceptual similarity coding was observed in parahippocampal cortex only when task demands biased attention to conceptual object features.
source: First, we see visual similarity coding in LOC only when task demands biased attention to visual object features, and conceptual similarity coding in parahippocampal cortex only when task demands biased attention to conceptual object features.
evidence: Summary of task-dependent effects in parahippocampal cortex

claim: There was a trend toward an interaction between behavior-based models and fMRI task context in perirhinal cortex.
source: Second, we saw a trend toward an interaction between behavior-based models and fMRI task context in PRC, such that visual similarity coding was more pronounced in the visual task context than was conceptual similarity coding, and vice versa.
evidence: Summary of statistical trend in PRC

claim: Attention appeared to modulate multi-voxel activity patterns rather than merely manifesting as univariate gain modulation.
source: Thus, attending to specific types of features did not merely manifest as univariate gain modulation. Rather, attention appeared to modulated multi-voxel activity patterns.
evidence: Inference drawn from pattern of task-dependent effects

claim: Parahippocampal cortex exhibited conceptual similarity coding in the conceptual task context.
source: Another novel aspect of our findings is that parahippocampal cortex exhibited conceptual similarity coding in the conceptual task context.
evidence: Summary of RSA results in parahippocampal cortex

claim: Parahippocampal cortex broadly contributes to cognition by processing contextual associations, including the co-occurrence of objects within a context.
source: Interestingly, it has been suggested that this structure broadly contributes to cognition by processing contextual associations, including the co-occurrence of objects within a context (Bar, 2004; Aminoff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior theoretical work

claim: Objects that regularly co-occur in the same context often share many conceptual features, but do not necessarily share many visual features.
source: Critically, objects that regularly co-occur in the same context (e.g. 'comb' and 'hairdryer' in a barbershop) often share many conceptual features (e.g. functional properties such as 'used to style hair'), but do not necessarily share many visual features.
evidence: Logical inference about relationship between co-occurrence and feature similarity

claim: Object-evoked responses in parahippocampal cortex may express feature-based conceptual similarity structure because objects with many shared conceptual features bring to mind an associated context.
source: Thus, object-evoked responses in parahippocampal cortex may express feature-based conceptual similarity structure because objects with many shared conceptual features bring to mind an associated context, whereas objects that are visually similar but conceptually distinct do not (e.g. hairdryer and gun).
evidence: Speculative inference about mechanism underlying parahippocampal cortex results

claim: Perirhinal cortex represented object concepts in a task-invariant, integrative similarity code that captured the visual and conceptual relatedness among stimuli.
source: Specifically, we revealed that PRC represented object concepts in a task-invariant, integrative similarity code that captured the visual and conceptual relatedness among stimuli.
evidence: Summary of main finding

claim: The neuroanatomical specificity of integrative coding in perirhinal cortex suggests that this region uniquely supports integration across visual and conceptual features.
source: Moreover, the striking neuroanatomical specificity of this result suggests that PRC uniquely supports integration across these fundamentally different types of features.
evidence: Inference drawn from searchlight analysis showing specificity to PRC

claim: The pattern of results implicates perirhinal cortex in the representation of fully-specified objects.

claim: All stimuli were presented as words to ensure that conceptual and visual features were extracted from pre-existing representations of object concepts.
source: Given our specific interest in understanding pre-existing representations of object concepts rather than bottom-up perceptual processing, all stimuli were presented as words. This approach ensured that conceptual and visual features were extracted from pre-existing representations of object concepts.
evidence: Methodological rationale for stimulus presentation format

claim: When words are used as stimuli, both conceptual and visual features are arbitrarily related to the physical input.
source: That is to say, both conceptual and visual features were arbitrarily related to the physical input (i.e. the orthography of the word).
evidence: Explanation of methodological rationale

claim: When pictures are used as stimuli, visual features are accessible from the pictorial cue, whereas conceptual features require abstraction from the cue.
source: By contrast, when pictures are used as stimuli, visual features are accessible from the pictorial cue, whereas conceptual features require abstraction from the cue.
evidence: Explanation of methodological rationale by contrast

claim: Across participants, 95.7% of catch trials were rated as being very similar.
source: Each participant was also presented with four catch trials on which an object concept was paired with itself. Across participants, 95.7% of catch trials were rated as being very similar.

source: A total of 4851 unique features were produced across all 80 object concepts and participants.

claim: Features listed by fewer than 4 out of 20 participants were considered unreliable and discarded, leaving 723 unique features.
source: Features listed by fewer than 4 out of 20 participants were considered to be unreliable and discarded for the purpose of all subsequent analyses, leaving 723 unique features.
evidence: Methodological description of data processing

claim: On average, each of the 80 object concepts was associated with 10.6 features.
source: On average, each of the 80 object concepts was associated with 10.6 features.

claim: A total of 58 features (8% of the total) that characterized visual form or color were removed from the conceptual similarity model.
source: In order to ensure that the semantic relationships captured by our conceptual similarity model were not influenced by verbal descriptions of visual attributes, we systematically removed features that characterized either visual form or color (e.g. 'is round' or 'is red'). Using these criteria a total of 58 features (8% of the total number of features provided) were removed.
evidence: Methodological description of data processing

claim: Inclusion of the 58 features that described color and visual form in the behavior-based conceptual RDM did not significantly alter its relationship with the behavior-based visual RDM.
source: Moreover, inclusion of the 58 features that described color and visual form in the behavior-based conceptual RDM did not significantly alter its relationship with the visual behavior-based visual RDM (Kendall's tau-a = 0.01, p=0.09).
evidence: Supplementary analysis confirming robustness of main finding
